Senses.PreferredTarget: originally, there is not a single thing

Senses.Note: Eight witnesses across multiple received traditions support one verse-line and its later tests; textual variation is explicit.

Occurrences.Kwic: 菩提本無樹，明鏡亦非臺；本來無一物，何處惹塵埃？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The received Zongbao edition of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (六祖大師法寶壇經), in the first section, explicitly introduces this as Huineng's verse (惠能偈曰). Huineng's third line says, ‘Originally, there is not a single thing,’ followed by ‘where could it attract dust?’

It preserves the variants ‘Bodhi originally is not a tree’ (菩提本非樹) and ‘why rely on wiping away dust?’ (何假拂塵埃).

Senses.Explanation: Originally, there is not a single thing is a received verse-line whose exhaustive denial is repeatedly transmitted, varied, challenged, and placed beside counter-statements. The received Zongbao Platform Sutra gives the line in Huineng’s verse, while other collections transmit different surrounding lines. The older Dunhuang wording lacks this exact headword, so the entry limits its claim to the received line and later transmissions. Dongshan Liangjie says that even stating it directly does not earn the robe and bowl. Huangbo Xiyun answers a question about no-thing by denying even “no,” Yulin Tongxiu sets the line beside Changqing’s exposed solitary body, and Zhongfeng criticizes conceptual interpretation of it. These tests block treating the line as a self-explaining theory.

The “original face” is the face a person is challenged to recognize or investigate before acquired distinctions settle the answer. The records repeatedly preserve Huineng’s question to Ming: when not thinking good and not thinking evil, “what is your original face?” (不思善不思惡，正恁麼時，如何是上座本來面目). Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes that question and the instruction to turn the light back upon one’s own original face. Guanyin Congxian deliberately removes the four words “original face” from Huineng’s demand and asks whether the alteration still belongs to Huineng’s lineage. Dahui Zonggao pairs the phrase with one’s home-ground scenery and says that the original face itself has never been deluded or awakened, locating delusion and awakening in a person’s momentary thought. Yulin Tongxiu tells the emperor to investigate the phrase in activity as well as stillness. Zhuanyu Guanheng equates the six sense-fields, when recollected without discrimination, with one’s own original face. Miyun Yuanwu urges recognition of it amid ordinary bending and looking up, then answers his own renewed question with a shout and a spatial saying. Yushan Shangsi makes his staff leap into a hall, knock down the person of no rank, and smash the original face in a deliberately extravagant hall address. Across these uses the phrase is a question, an object of investigation and recognition, an explicit equation, and a target of corrective wordplay; no single verbal reply is made its universal definition.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 1,493 hits in 285 files representing 281 independent works. Seven curated occurrences from seven independent works meet the depth floor. Parallel versions of Tianyin’s record and Yulin’s exchange in later anthologies were not counted as additional evidence.

Senses.Explanation: One’s proper part is what belongs to the person or office without borrowing an external performance. Speakers apply it to a monastic, a matter, implements, conduct, and the work expected here; the surrounding noun decides whether English needs “proper,” “genuine,” or “one’s own.”

In Chan interview and instruction, the compound names the matter proper to the person rather than an item borrowed from authoritative predecessors. Zhaozhou Congshen says a lineage teacher must receive people with it, while an unnamed monk’s question about it is answered by pointing the matter back to the questioner. Baichi Yuanshuo places inquiry, eating, bodily functions, and ordinary activity within one’s own matter but still demands that it be stated directly. Danxia Dangui warns that merely speaking of it has already made it extraneous, and Xiuyelin defines it as where one’s own root-destiny comes to rest. Bai Juyi challenges a scripture-reciting monk about a cleric’s own matter. Yuanwu Keqin says that even cloudless clarity in it cannot simply be let pass. Nanquan Puyuan likewise demands it directly without pointing east or west. Across these uses, the phrase marks what cannot be outsourced or replaced by discursive display, while remaining a demand made in concrete encounters rather than an imported abstract teaching.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 975 hits in 205 files and 201 independent works. Eight exact witnesses across seven independent works meet the packet floor; the work-based count prevents two volumes of one work from being treated as independent sources.

SearchAliases: the case one is working on
Senses.Explanation: The saying, question, or public case singled out as a person's main subject of inquiry. The possessives and verbal predicates in later Chinese Chan records make this local use concrete. Jiexian tells a hall leader to know each person's own word or saying under primary investigation; another passage says that not knowing it leaves the leader without a way to act. Zhanran Yuancheng tells people to place the selected saying before their eyes, Konggu Daocheng says to raise it, and Langting Jingting warns Qianyun that he has dropped one line of it behind his head. The compound can take 'public case' or 'word, saying, conversational thread' after it, and can itself be said to be broken through. Yongzheng asks, 'What is primary investigation?' and gives one particular example: if one trusts the gate of recollecting buddha, investigate who is recollecting buddha. Wuyi Yuanlai says that the Chan house relies on primary investigation and that when it breaks through it is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. These predicates describe the assigned subject and the act of investigating it without turning the term into a named system.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 232 matches in 100 files. The expanded phrase 'word or saying under primary investigation' has eighty-nine matches in fifty files; 'raise the primary investigation' has twenty matches in fifteen; 'public case of primary investigation' has four in four; and 'one line of primary investigation' has three in three. One text has the only direct 'what is primary investigation?' formula and its own example; two texts use 'the so-called primary investigation.' The phrase is strongly possessive: texts say 'each person's,' 'one's own,' 'the one assigned,' and 'not knowing his.' No evidence supports treating it as an untranslated foreign object or as a person-specific sense.

Senses.Explanation: A person's native ground is that person's own ground, most often deployed in the fixed phrase “native-ground scenery.” Records say to recognize one's original face and tread one's native-ground scenery, warn that wrong roads conceal each person's native-ground scenery, and ask that it be illuminated or fully seen through. A preface says the records return to the person's own native-ground scenery; teaching-seat records place it in bowing, turning, daily activity, or the lifting of a staff. The corpus treats this ground and its scenery as something belonging to each person and subject to public demand and display. It does not define it as a metaphysical substrate.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use “original landscape” for what is disclosed as one's own, often pairing it with the original face and contrasting its presence with seeking outside, clinging to purity, or remaining blocked by distinctions. Yuanwu Keqin and Dahui Zonggao place the expression beside the original face and say it is present through ordinary modes of activity or belongs to each person. Mi'an Xianjie says it suddenly appears when inquiry reaches the end of explanations, while Tianyin Yuanxiu says paired categories such as illumination and function appear upon this landscape. Jie'an Wujin's verse says it was never sought outside and is not absent in walking, sitting, or lying down. Zhongfeng Mingben provocatively says dullness and distraction are wholly this landscape, but immediately warns that merely accepting that formulation is another error. Sanyi Mingyu likewise denies that settling into undifferentiated purity is the original landscape.

The mind identified in a record as original or fundamental. The word occurs 748 times in 157 allowlisted texts. The Mirror Record says mind has no form, color, root, lodging, arising, extinction, or observable contemplation; if something observable can be carried out, that text assigns it to reception, conception, activity, and discrimination rather than original mind. The Platform Record pairs recognizing one’s original mind with seeing one’s original nature (若識自本心，見自本性). Other records say it is neither joined nor separate, reject the claim that it first needs stillness, and place original nature and original mind together. These are differing corpus predicates of one textual term, not a menu of interpretations.
Senses.Note: Primary corpus-wide original-mind sense. Cross-check original nature (本性), true mind, and no-mind as neighboring entries with their own predicates. No single imported metaphysical definition is imposed.

Senses.Explanation: One's nature as it is from the outset. Chan records repeatedly use 'see one's own original nature' beside 'recognize one's own original mind.' The Platform Record makes seeing it the distinction between remaining outside the gate and entering, and describes it as not arising or extinguishing. The Mirror Record says that original nature has no difference and is not obtained because of conduct. These are the texts' recorded descriptions; the English should preserve the plain noun phrase rather than substitute a later explanatory system. The omitted collocation "original nature empty" (本性空) occurs forty times in thirty texts, but it has more than one syntax. Twenty-seven occurrences in twenty-five texts belong to the fixed line, "understand body and mind, original nature empty; how would this person differ from buddha?" (了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別). A later Chan address raises that line and immediately comments, "the buddha-body is neither real nor empty; buddha-as-appearance is not appearance" (佛身無實亦無虗，佛幻非幻). The Source-Mirror Record gives a separate explicit definition: "as for original-nature empty, it is the own-nature clear-and-clean mind; original nature is own nature; empty means clear and clean" (本性空者，即是自性清淨心；本性即自性；空，即清淨義).
Senses.Note: The corpus has 667 matches in 152 files. The compound occurs in direct corrections, statements linking it with original mind, and descriptions of it as without difference. Six matches in six files explicitly pair original nature and original mind. The evidence supports one corpus-wide sense. The forty "original nature empty" matches are therefore not treated as forty copies of one bare equation. The fixed body-and-mind verse, the Source-Mirror definition, and the critical construction "rely on original-nature empty" (恃本性空, two occurrences in two texts) are distinct deployments. One Source-Mirror list criticizes people who follow binding impulses while relying on original-nature empty, alongside people who cling to coverings and wrongly add removal and severing (或隨結使而恃本性空，或執纏蓋而妄加除斷). Each predicate is reported as that text's wording rather than generalized beyond its occurrence.

Senses.Explanation: “Fundamentally, not one thing” occurs as assertion, verse line, and interview question; the records place it beside what can be presented, displayed, or investigated. Literally, ‘fundamentally, not one thing.’ The exact shorter phrase occurs 34 times in 30 allowlisted texts. Yangshan's record predicates it of one's own mind-source and contrasts immediate recognition there with gradual certification through myriad deeds. Yinyuan Longqi says there is fundamentally not one thing to present. Yulin Tongxiu places three heads, six arms, a thousand hands, and a thousand eyes beside the statement that fundamentally there is not one thing, while also saying the myriad forms run crosswise. In a public exchange, Miyin is asked what the student investigates if fundamentally there is not one thing and answers, ‘take yourself out.’ Huineng's longer ‘originally, not one thing’ is a close morphological family form, preserved as family evidence rather than counted as the exact headword. The shorter phrase is thus a predicate, verse line, and publicly tested proposition, not an imported metaphysical definition.

Senses.Explanation: It appears in the Platform Record's list of Huineng's statements on the nature: "who expected the nature to be from the start pure … from the start complete … able to produce the myriad things?" (何期自性本自清淨；何期自性本自具足；何期自性能生萬法). The corpus also turns the wording into a direct question: "what is complete from the start?" The recorded answer is, "because not one thing can be obtained, it is called complete" (因無一物可得，所以說具足). A prose criticism asks, "complete from the start—who picks it up or puts it down?" (本自具足，阿誰拈起放下). Other records set the phrase against outside acquisition: living beings are complete from the start and "do not depend on seeking outside" (不假外求). The Zen deployment therefore joins the phrase to the nature, direct questioning, the impossibility of picking it up or putting it down, and explicit refusal of outside acquisition; this entry reports those statements without converting them into a system of cultivation.

Senses.Explanation: The myriad things return to one: the opening clause of a stock public question (萬法歸一). It most often forms the first clause of the stock question, 'The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一；一歸何處). In Zhaozhou Congshen's case the answer is: 'When I was in Qingzhou; I made a cloth shirt, weighing seven catties' (我在青州；作一領布衫，重七斤). The corpus preserves other answers without making any of them a dictionary gloss: Wenshu Yingzhen says, 'The Yellow River has nine bends' (黃河九曲); Baizhang Mingzhao An says, 'There has not been a single person who did not ask' (未有一箇人不問); Shending Yikui answers the first clause with 'rain comes, the mountain colors darken' (雨來山色暗), then answers the second with 'clouds clear, the moon is newer' (雲淨月彌新). The phrase is therefore not merely a proposition. Zen records bend it into the opening move of a portable public-interview case whose second clause and sharply speaker-specific answers must remain attached. Juelang Daosheng answers the inherited question by challenging who taught the monk to ask it; Zhean Fan raises the Zhaozhou version and comments on its pressure. Both keep the headword as the first clause of the same public question.
Senses.Note: The exact four-character string occurs 955 times in 236 allowlisted storage files. The unpunctuated full question occurs 56 times in 22 files, while its second clause occurs 838 times in 216. Standard self-definition searches yielded no direct definition; their zero results are recorded in WORK rather than printed as unattested Chinese evidence. The attested question, the label for Zhaozhou's case, and later verse headings share one referent. Answers remain attached to their respective speakers and do not become additional senses of the headword.
